source.title: Time-Aware Feature Selection: Adaptive Temporal Masking for Stable Sparse Autoencoder Training

page_placements.theme: Absorption depends on the SAE objective and architecture, not only on size or sparsity

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature absorption under several SAE training methods and reports that the amount varies by method. It does not sweep dictionary size or test the proposed feature-splitting geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an absorption score using a first-letter classification and probe-projection procedure, including aggregate scores and e-word scores. Those results are recorded below. Comparisons or values from cited work are not included. Dictionary width is fixed, and the paper does not report a coarse-to-fine feature partition or geometric family analysis.
record.test_reason: Absorption is measured with Chanin et al.'s first-letter probe-projection metric on Gemma-2-2B. That is the same method and measure as a V4 original, applied to four SAE training methods at one width (n=16384, layer 12). The study's aim is its own method (ATM), but the comparator SAEs give direct absorption rates in SAEs trained normally. Splitting itself (V1–V3, V5) is not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that ATM cuts absorption about 40% relative to the best existing method (JumpReLU) while keeping reconstruction quality. They also claim superior sparse probing, though Table 1 shows TopK higher (0.7698 vs 0.7161). They present ATM as yielding more stable, interpretable features.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes Adaptive Temporal Masking and compares its absorption score with TopK, JumpReLU, and standard SAEs at one fixed dictionary width. It uses a probe-based absorption measure described as following Chanin et al.; it does not reproduce a dictionary-size splitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Absorption score varies across SAE methods; the paper also reports separate overall and e-word results. Model, layer, and dictionary width are fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed width, absorption rate varies about 20-fold across SAE training objectives: ATM 0.0068 vs TopK 0.1402. The comparison is confounded by large L0 differences.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The rate of feature absorption depends on the SAE training objective (not just size or sparsity), and alternative objectives can reduce it.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to Gemma-2-2B, layer 12, and one dictionary width; the authors state that compute constraints prevented larger-model and systematic hyperparameter evaluations. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The methods section gives EMA decay β = 0.9, while the experimental setup gives β = 0.99.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported absorption results were omitted. Other metrics in Table 1 do not measure absorption or feature splitting.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep; no coarse-to-fine feature replacement, coverage or direction analysis.
No splitting measurement; one model, one layer, one width; no open SAE releases.
No feature families, geometry or concept-hierarchy analysis.

The clause that changing SAE size or sparsity doesn't fix absorption: width is fixed and there is no controlled L0 sweep. Methods differ in L0 by about 200x, which is confounded with method. No direct parent/child latent coverage analysis.
No cross-size latent decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
No splitting measurement, no correlated/hierarchical input manipulation, no Matryoshka SAE. Only absorption is compared across objectives.

missing.what: L0 sparsity per method (ATM 3280, TopK 40, JumpReLU 2666, SAE 8724). Needed as a condition on every absorption row, since density likely drives the absorption differences.
Standard SAE e-word absorption score and per-letter scores behind the claim that the reduction is 'consistent across token categories'. These are not reported numerically.

record.verdict_notes: The absorption comparison is heavily confounded: ATM, JumpReLU and the standard SAE are extremely dense (L0 in the thousands of 16384), while TopK has L0=40. All SAEs were trained on only 5M tokens. Low absorption in the dense SAEs may reflect density rather than ATM's mechanism. There are no uncertainty estimates and only a single run. EMA β is inconsistent (0.9 in Methods vs 0.99 in Setup). V6 links were removed because the rows measure absorption, not splitting; the objective-dependence finding is listed under fits_no_version. Workshop paper.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size sweep; no measurement of whether smaller-dictionary features are replaced by finer features that cover their inputs or lie near their direction.
Tests only Gemma-2-2B at one layer and one dictionary width; no large-model or open-release comparison, and no splitting measurement.
No measurement of nested feature families, geometric proximity, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy.

Measures absorption with the paper's probe-based score, but does not directly test parent-child activation coverage, sweep SAE size or sparsity, or establish whether changing size or sparsity fixes absorption.
No comparison of latent combinations across dictionary sizes and no assessment of novel latents or canonical units.

Compares absorption scores across SAE methods, including the proposed training method, but does not establish that splitting is an artifact of the objective, test hierarchical or correlated inputs as the cause, measure what the model's own units are, or test Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: Comparator SAEs give absorption measurements bearing on V4. Weak, since method and L0 are confounded.

tranche.reason: Uses Chanin et al.'s first-letter probe-projection absorption metric on SAEs of four training methods, so same method and measure. Its aim is its own method. The reader's T5 is not needed because the paper makes no argument against any version.

source_check.notes: One run per method: n=16384, layer 12, 5M WikiText tokens, no seeds or uncertainty, method confounded with L0. TopK reconstructs far worse (explained variance 0.6016 vs 0.73-0.98), so the short training may limit the comparators. The conclusion's 'superior sparse probing' contradicts Table 1 (TopK 0.7698 > ATM 0.7161).

statements.problem: Gives no number for this study and does not name it; it only cites r2 and r6 (TopK, L0 40). Those rows do show sizable absorption at one width.
None. All four values and L0s match Table 1, and the statement and its conditions say method and L0 are confounded in this study.

statements.correction: ATM L0 3280: 0.0068; JumpReLU L0 2666: 0.0114; standard L1 SAE L0 8724: 0.0161; TopK L0 40: 0.1402. All at n=16384, layer 12, 5M tokens. Method and L0 vary together; no within-method L0 sweep. Among the dense SAEs the highest L0 (8724) has the highest absorption (0.0161).
statements.problem: Numbers right, but it lists this study as evidence that higher L0 reduces absorption without the method confound. The study cannot attribute the drop to L0.

statements.correction: ATM 0.0068 vs TopK 0.1402 at n=16384, layer 12. L0 is 3280 (ATM) vs 40 (TopK), given only in Table 1. The study does not discuss the L0 confound.
statements.problem: The ratio is right (0.1402/0.0068 is about 20.6). But the study never mentions L0 or any confound. That is the catalog's reading, not the study's.
